problem: "Two processes cannot read each other's memory" is false as written. The same chapter later shows two ways they can: shared memory (Section 2) maps the same physical pages into both, and ptrace (Section 3) reads and writes another process's memory. The intended point is only that processes do not share an address space by default, so the sentence as written will confuse a student who has just read Sections 2 and 3.
fix: "Two processes have separate address spaces by default, so they meet inside the kernel."

problem: Calling a socket "a pipe with an address" / "the same idea but addressed" suggests a socket is still one-way like a pipe. A connected SOCK_STREAM socket (AF_UNIX or AF_INET) is bidirectional: both ends can read and write. The addressing is not the only difference.
fix: "A socket is an addressed, bidirectional byte stream; a pipe is one-way and has no address."

problem: waitpid on a stopped tracee does not "reap" it. It reports the stop (WIFSTOPPED); the tracee is still alive and only becomes reapable when it later exits.
fix: "the tracee must first be attached and its stop collected with waitpid; until then ptrace calls return ESRCH."

problem: The arithmetic is right only because the page size is taken as 4096 bytes. The default is 16 pages, so on a kernel built with larger pages the same ring holds more than 65536 bytes. The buffer size is also changeable at run time with fcntl(F_SETPIPE_SZ), which the chapter never mentions and a student may assume is impossible.
fix: Add: "On the usual 4 KiB page this gives 65536 bytes; with a larger page the same 16-page ring is bigger. The size can be changed with fcntl(fd, F_SETPIPE_SZ, n)."
